first_impression.reaction: Went straight to the FAQ, as I always do. Every answer names GIA, so I went back up to the top. The intro tells me what I won't get: "No grading tables, no prices, no rules." Fair enough, at least it's upfront. Then "Just proportion, preference and light" is a bit of a mood line. I'll put up with it because the sources are real.

journey.quote: GIA says a marquise often looks larger face-up than a round diamond of the same carat weight.
journey.reaction: Good. It's a specific claim with a named source I can check myself, and it's what I'd actually want to know.

journey.quote: This is about appearance, not value.
journey.reaction: Nobody's trying to sell me anything there. That's the kind of caveat that makes me trust the rest of it.

journey.quote: GIA grades cut only on round brilliants, and every other shape is classed as a fancy shape.
journey.reaction: Useful. That's a real trade-off. If I buy an oval, there's no cut grade to fall back on when I'm haggling.

journey.quote: GIA gives no hand or finger guidance for the cushion, so the honest answer is to try it on.
journey.reaction: It admits where the evidence runs out instead of filling the gap with fluff. Good.

journey.quote: No grading tables, no prices, no rules.
journey.reaction: I'm a finance guy buying a ring. My next question is whether some shapes cost more per carat than others, and the page won't say a word about money. Honest, but it leaves my main question open.
Revived since when? The marquise section mentions Louis XV but says nothing about a revival. It's a small thing, but it's the only label in the table I can't trace back to the text.

journey.section: From the ring to the destination
journey.quote: When you are ready to plan, Wedded Concierge looks after venue, travel, vendors and payments anywhere in the world, with one Wedded Advisor as your single point of contact from start to finish.
journey.reaction: Fine, here's the pitch. After all that careful sourcing it's suddenly a broad claim with no proof, no fee and no example. "Payments" makes me wonder straight away who's getting paid and how.

unanswered_questions: Do some shapes cost more or less per carat than others? Even a sourced general direction would do.
How does Wedded Concierge charge: flat fee, percentage, or commission from venues and vendors?
When the concierge 'looks after payments', do I pay suppliers directly or through you, and is there a mark-up?
Is there a real wedding I can look at with the actual budget?

turn_offs_found.quote: Wedded Concierge looks after venue, travel, vendors and payments anywhere in the world
turn_offs_found.why: It's a sweeping service claim with no evidence, fee model or example, and it sits right next to a page where everything else is sourced.

turn_offs_found.quote: Have a shape in mind and a place forming in your head? A Wedded Advisor is happy to talk it through, from the first idea onwards.
turn_offs_found.why: Soft emotional nudge to finish. It's harmless, but it gives me nothing to go on.

would_share_with: My partner, if we're arguing about oval versus round

cta_reaction.quote: You can talk to a Wedded Concierge about a proposal or wedding abroad.
cta_reaction.why: I came here for ring shapes, not a planner. To be fair, the CTA comes after the evidence, not before it. But I'm not enquiring with a planner until I can see how they get paid and whether they take a cut from venues. This page doesn't touch on that.

top_3_changes: Back up the concierge paragraph or tone it down. Link to a page that explains the fee model and whether suppliers pay commission, or at least say how payments are handled.
Add one sourced line on whether shape affects price per carat, or say plainly that it's out of scope and link to where it's covered.
Change 'Historic, revived' in the table to something the body text backs up, e.g. 'Historic, dramatic'.

checks.check: Every journey point and turn-off has an exact quote from the draft
No invented brand facts; missing fee and commission info logged as unanswered questions
HTML comments and fact markers treated as invisible

assumptions: Daniel is reading as a groom choosing a ring, not as someone actively shortlisting planners for this search.
